rewrites.summary:
Castilla y León is the only Spanish autonomous community that has never enacted a regional LGTBI or gender-identity law, and for a transgender visitor that vacuum has a practical administrative meaning: no dedicated regional equality office exists to receive a complaint, there is no institutional hate-crime observatory, and no region-specific administrative protocol governs responses to gender-motivated incidents. No criminal ban or facility restriction exists in the region, national criminal law fully applies, and the severity floor is therefore set by the state; the recorded deviation of approximately −0.07 from the national score (0.88) reflects sub-national administrative coldness and rural exposure rather than any region-specific criminal threat.

The pending regional LGTBI+ equality bill (registered December 2024, in processing since 11 June 2025) is framed around ending the sexilio — the documented exodus of LGBT people, especially the young, from the region's rural areas to larger cities — a resident-facing concern rather than a visitor protection; until it is enacted, a transgender traveller facing discrimination has no dedicated regional channel beyond the national institutions, and the protective infrastructure is thinnest in the rural areas where the exodus pattern is documented.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Legislative flux: the bill proposed by the opposition PSOE group reached processing on 11 June 2025 only after the governing PP abstained and Vox voted alone against; Vox is on record rejecting LGTBI subsidies in the region, and LGBTI advocates fear the process could stall in committee.

Neighbour comparisons: Madrid (0.84), which at least operated a trans law and a law against anti-LGBT hostility before narrowing them, shows a rollback pattern this region never had a framework to narrow; the other two non-legislating communities, Ceuta and Melilla (0.85), present a statute-book-only gap with no incident evidence, whereas the larger deviation of Castilla y León rests on its documented rural-exodus pattern compounding the absence of protective infrastructure.
rewrites.localsOnly: The sexilio pattern is resident-facing in its essentials: a documented exodus of LGBT people, especially the young, from the region's rural areas to larger cities, sustained by the same vacuum a visitor would notice — no regional equality office, hate-crime observatory or administrative protocol for residents' complaints. The pending LGTBI+ equality bill answers regional LGBTI+ collectives' long-standing demands, while a visitor's exposure stays governed by state law.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Whether the pending bill advances or stalls in committee was unresolved at reporting time. No visitor documents, border-screening practice, or marriage/partner-travel finding specific to this region is recorded in the dossier.

rewrites.summary:
Ceuta, an autonomous city rather than a comunidad autónoma, has no regional LGTBI or gender-identity statute — a framework gap it shares with its neighbouring city Melilla and with Castilla y León, recorded in the national regional-law inventories as a gap case only. No incident evidence, no enforcement data and no hate-offence figure separating the city from the national aggregate was retrievable, so this is a statute-book gap, explicitly not an incident finding. National criminal law and the national police still operate here, so the enforcement floor for a transgender visitor is unchanged from the rest of the country; unlike some communities, the city has no regional equality office, LGTBI observatory or police force of its own.

The border-fence crossing environment and the city's religious-minority composition create a document-and-presentation context different from the rest of the country, adding modest friction for a visitor whose identity documents do not match presentation. The one LGTBI-specific episode the dossier records for the city concerns migrants remaining there after an irregular-entry wave, not visitor incidents.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
National-inventory context: the 2025 national review of LGTBI+ policy names this city, its neighbouring community and two other regions as the only regions still without a specific law on promotion of LGTBI+ rights, and records June 2025 legislative progress in two of those regions with no equivalent step recorded for these two autonomous cities; a 2020 precedent study placed both cities at the tail of trans-student recognition and protection rankings.

Community comparisons: two other communities in the parent nation — the Basque Country and Navarra — each operate a regional equality office, an LGTBI observatory and a police force of their own, institutions the two autonomous cities lack.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing facts: the 2020 precedent study placed this autonomous city and its neighbouring community at the tail of trans-student recognition and protection rankings — education-policy data for residents. The documented LGTBI-specific episode concerns LGTBI+ migrants remaining in the city after thousands entered irregularly on 30–31 July: an LGTBI+ association wrote to the national migration authority demanding their urgent transfer to the rest of the country, calling transfer 'the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion' and citing their 'extreme vulnerability', and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for them.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No incident evidence, enforcement data or hate-offence figure separating the city from the national aggregate was retrievable; the absence of counts is uninformative rather than reassuring, and the finding remains a statute-book gap, explicitly not an incident finding. No visitor documents, border-screening or marriage/partner-travel finding specific to the city beyond the border-fence context is recorded in the dossier.

rewrites.summary:
Melilla, like its neighbouring city Ceuta, is an autonomous city with no regional LGTBI or gender-identity statute — the sole sub-national finding for the city is this framework-only gap: no incident evidence, no enforcement data and no per-city hate-offence figure was retrievable, so the absence of counts is uninformative rather than reassuring. National criminal law and the national police still apply; the city's reporting infrastructure for gender-motivated incidents is thinner than in the larger communities, and no regional rollback or opposition pattern is documented: the finding is purely legislative silence.

For a transgender visitor the enforcement floor is therefore the national one, and the city's religious-demographic composition and border environment parallel its neighbouring city's, though the crossing friction is less pronounced here.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Framework context from the national page that supplies the law a visitor stands under: same-sex marriage and adoption nationwide since July 2005; hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity banned since 1995 with penalty enhancements for such motives; and legal-gender self-determination on documents without surgery or sterilisation since the trans law approved 16 February 2023. The only local datapoint on that page is a 2008 registry for unmarried same-sex couples in Melilla — alongside its neighbouring city and all the other communities of the country — granting benefits the page calls mainly symbolic; it is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute, consistent with the legislative-silence finding of this record.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing facts: the national inventories record that this autonomous city and its neighbouring city have no regional LGTBI statutes and rely on the national framework and central-government equality policies; the 2008 registry for unmarried same-sex couples is the only documented legal item applying to resident couples, with benefits the source calls mainly symbolic. No resident discrimination data, recognition practice or education-ranking detail specific to Melilla appears in the dossier.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The absence of incident counts, enforcement data and per-city hate-offence figures is uninformative rather than reassuring, and whether the thinner reporting infrastructure reflects fewer incidents or fewer reports is unresolved from the dossier. No visitor documents, border-screening or marriage/partner-travel finding specific to the city beyond the mainly-symbolic 2008 registry is recorded.

rewrites.summary:
In May 2025 the city authority of the state capital erected anti-homosexuality warning signboards at several locations, including near youth-frequented areas around a state university; when criticised, a state executive councillor publicly confirmed the installations were deliberate, framing them as a 'constant reminder' to steer people away from homosexuality. A transgender activist and, on 14 May 2025, thirteen civil-society organisations led by a national trans-rights group demanded removal, calling the boards discriminatory hate speech.

The state also retains hudud-style penal provisions (2002) that remain inoperative because a federal statute caps the sentences the state religious courts may impose — confirmed current in a 2026 review — while discretionary religious-law offences and the national criminal prohibition of same-sex conduct do apply. What a transgender visitor meets here is open, ongoing official hostility, including state-level endorsement of anti-homosexual messaging, without any trans-status-specific criminalisation documented in the surviving sources.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The national-legal interplay frames the position: the federal sentencing cap is what keeps the 2002 provisions inoperative, and the surviving sources confirm the state religious-court offences and the national same-sex-conduct prohibition stand. No comparison with neighbouring states and no national policy turbulence beyond this framework is documented in the dossier.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing reaction: on 14 May 2025 thirteen civil-society organisations, led by a national trans-rights group, urged the city authority to remove the signboards, condemning them as discriminatory and a violation of international human-rights law, and criticised the executive councillor's defence of the boards as inciting hatred and discrimination against LGBTQ people. The signboards target residents' conduct and environment — placed at locations including areas frequented by young people around a university — with the official framing presented as a 'constant reminder' directed at the state's residents.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Whether trans-status-specific enforcement exists beyond the general same-sex-conduct provisions is not documented in the surviving sources; the record carries no trans-specific criminalisation finding. Post-2023 state government crackdown rhetoric was found only in secondary reports, so its weight is unverifiable from the dossier. No visitor documents, border-screening or marriage/partner-travel finding specific to this state is recorded.

rewrites.summary:
In October 2020 a private birthday party was raided and 30 transgender women were singled out from the gathering and arrested, while the event's organiser was separately investigated for 'encouraging vice'. The raid's design — isolating transgender women as a category from a mixed party — evidences enforcement capacity and willingness aimed at transgender people specifically. A coalition of national human-rights organisations publicly protested, identifying a pattern of punishing organisers and allies of trans people rather than only trans people themselves.

The legal baseline for a visitor: the state's 2014 religious criminal enactment criminalises same-sex conduct (liable to fines, imprisonment or whipping) and criminalises a male posing as a woman in public, while female cross-dressing is not criminalised; a transgender visitor whose public presentation does not match her assigned sex is directly exposed under that provision, and same-sex conduct offences apply to a visiting couple as they do to residents.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: No national policy turbulence, litigation flux or comparison with neighbouring states beyond the framework itself is documented in the dossier: the sources date from 2020, and the record documents no later state-specific incident series.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing enforcement pattern: the 2020 raid singled out trans women from a mixed private gathering of residents, and the coalition identified a trend of punishing organisers and allies of trans people rather than only trans people themselves. The 2014 enactment also provides that women convicted of same-sex-conduct offences may be committed to an approved home for a further period — a resident sanction detail.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The surviving sources date from 2020, so the continuity or intensity of enforcement since then is unverified from the dossier. No visitor documents, border-screening or marriage/partner-travel finding specific to this state is recorded; the penalties of the 2014 enactment are the only quantified legal detail available.

The national-framework page's dedicated section for this state/province reports the 2014 religious criminal enactment: same-sex conduct between men and between women is criminalised, punishable by fines, up to three years' imprisonment, or up to six strokes of whipping; a male posing as a woman in public is criminalised with a smaller fine or up to one year's imprisonment, while female cross-dressing is not; women convicted of the women-with-women offence may additionally be committed to an approved home for up to six months. rewrites.summary:
Aguascalientes sits under the national framework: no criminalisation of same-sex conduct or trans presence, while legal gender recognition nationally remains a state-by-state mosaic that the national courts have pressed legislatures to complete. No state-level recognition law, no hostile ordinances and no state-specific enforcement or incident series is documented in the surviving audited sources.

The one state-specific legal development is the national supreme court's April 2026 ruling that the state's civil-code requirements for changing the gender marker on birth certificates — judicial or ministerial intervention, civil trials, probative proof of identity and marginal annotations — are discriminatory and violate privacy; the court ordered the state's civil registry to grant recognition through a simple, confidential administrative procedure honouring self-perception, with a new birth certificate issued and no marginal notes revealing a prior gender. The ruling's immediate effect is limited to persons represented by the civil association that filed it, so the general position for a transgender visitor is unchanged: no enacted recognition procedure covering the general public, and no documented incidents in the surviving sources.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Litigation flux: the April 2026 supreme court ruling is the operative legal development, and the broader pattern of the national courts pressing legislatures to complete recognition frames the mosaic; the capital's 2024 transfemicide law is the reform benchmark used to contrast the capital and pioneer states with the non-reforming majority, which includes this state.

Inventory context: an international human-rights organisation's March 2025 survey records this state among the states that have not reformed at all, and its 2024 reference-case report documents the human-rights cost of the absence of legal gender recognition in non-reforming states.
rewrites.localsOnly:
No legal gender recognition procedure has ever been enacted in this state (listed by the international human-rights organisation in March 2025 among states that have not reformed at all), and state anti-discrimination protection for sexual orientation and gender identity remains an unpassed initiative (February 2025) — resident-facing gaps that do not move a visitor's deviation from the national position.

Resident discrimination data: a regional newspaper (23 August 2026) reports local activists saying conversion-therapy operations still run in the state under the guise of addiction-treatment annexes despite the legal prohibition, that a person who escaped one of these spaces arrived at the group the previous year, and that trans women continue to suffer prejudice-motivated aggression; a national survey shows 7.3% of the state's population aged 15 and over self-identifying as LGBTI+, the fifth-highest proportion among the nation's states.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Two of the international human-rights organisation's pages were not retrievable at fetch time (one blocked, one uncached), so those claims rest on the known content of the underlying reports rather than a fresh fetch. The April 2026 court order's operationalisation — how quickly the civil registry implements the administrative procedure for people beyond the filing association's clients — is unverified from the dossier. No visitor documents, border-screening or marriage/partner-travel finding specific to this state beyond the ruling context is recorded.

The state's elected congress created an administrative legal gender recognition procedure by civil-code reform in 2021; after the national supreme court ruled in June 2023 that excluding children and adolescents was unconstitutional, a 2024 reform expanded the right to children, adolescents and non-binary people. Baja California Sur also recognises the transfemicide offence.

No region-specific incident or enforcement pattern was found in the audited sources, and visitor-facing risk tracks the national baseline: no local legal hostility is documented, and the recognition procedure itself is resident-facing civil-registry machinery.

rewrites.summary:
Campeche is among the Mexican states that have embraced the reform direction: its elected congress passed a 2024 civil-code reform creating an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, following rulings of the national supreme court pressing states to provide one. Identity documents can therefore be aligned locally without litigation — the single most visitor-relevant legal fact in a country where mismatched documents drive questioning and denials.

Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and no hostile ordinances or enforcement incidents against trans people appear in the audited sources. National context remains violent for trans people, and other states' transfemicide laws (the capital's 2024 statute being the benchmark) frame reform elsewhere; Campeche's own record in the surviving sources is defined by its recognition procedure rather than by documented incidents.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Litigation flux: the national supreme court's rulings pressing states to provide recognition procedures are the driver, and the capital's 2024 transfemicide statute — sentences up to 70 years, obliging the attorney general's office to publish statistics on crimes against the LGBTQ+ community — is the reform benchmark for other states; the same report notes over 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022. The national inventory counts 22 of 32 states with an administrative recognition procedure, of which Campeche is one.
rewrites.localsOnly: The 2024 legal gender recognition reform and transfemicide-offence recognition are resident-facing civil-registry and criminal-law machinery.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No hostile ordinances or enforcement incidents are documented — the absence of a signal is not proof of no enforcement. Whether the state's civil registry already operates the administrative procedure in practice, and how smoothly, is not documented in the audited sources. No visitor documents, border-screening or marriage/partner-travel finding specific to the state beyond the recognition-reform context is recorded.
